questions.question_text: The intermediates in heteropolar reactions are
questions.question_html: The intermediates in heteropolar reactions are

options.label: A
options.html: Free radicals only

options.label: D
options.html: Both anions and cations

questions.explanation_text: In heteropolar reactions, the bond breaks or forms in such a way that the electron pair goes to one atom. This gives charged species. For example, in heterolytic bond fission: $A-B \rightarrow A^{+}+B^{-}$ So the intermediates formed can be positive ions, called cations, or negative ions, called anions. Free radicals are formed in homolytic bond fission, not in heteropolar reactions. Hence, the correct option is: $\text{Option D: Both anions and cations}$
questions.explanation_html:
In heteropolar reactions, the bond breaks or forms in such a way that the electron pair goes to one atom. This gives charged species.

For example, in heterolytic bond fission:

$A-B \rightarrow A^{+}+B^{-}$

So the intermediates formed can be positive ions, called cations, or negative ions, called anions.

Free radicals are formed in homolytic bond fission, not in heteropolar reactions.

Hence, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D: Both anions and cations}$

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the strongest base?
questions.question_html: Which of the following is the strongest base?
questions.explanation_text: We know, an anion is strongest base, if its conjugate acid is weakest. Here, $CH_{3}COO^{-}$ will have conjugate acid $CH_{3}COOH$ . $Cl^{-}$ will have conjugate acid $HCl$ . $OH^{-}$ will have conjugate acid $HOH$ . $CH_{3}O^{-}$ will have conjugate acid $CH_{3}OH$ . Since, out of above four, $CH_{3}OH$ will be the weakest acid and hence, $CH_{3}O^{-}$ will be strongest base.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.question_text: Which of the following is more basic than aniline?
questions.question_html: Which of the following is more basic than aniline?
questions.explanation_text: Let's analyze each option by considering the availability of the nitrogen's lone pair for accepting a proton: $\text{Aniline:}C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}$ In aniline, the lone pair on nitrogen is partially delocalized into the benzene ring. This delocalization makes the lone pair less available for protonation, so aniline is less basic compared to amines where the lone pair is fully localized. $\text{Diphenylamine:}C_{6}H_{5}NHC_{6}H_{5}$ Here, the nitrogen is bonded to two phenyl groups. The lone pair can be delocalized into both aromatic rings, decreasing its availability even more than in aniline. This makes diphenylamine less basic. $\text{Triphenylamine:}N(C_{6}H_{5})_{3}$ In triphenylamine, the nitrogen is bonded to three phenyl groups, which further delocalizes the lone pair into the aromatic rings. As a result, the lone pair is even less available, making triphenylamine even less basic. $\text{Benzylamine:}C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}NH_{2}$ In benzylamine, the nitrogen is attached to a methylene group ( $CH_{2}$ ) before connecting to the benzene ring. This extra methylene group breaks the conjugation between the benzene ring and the amine, keeping the lone pair localized on the nitrogen. Being more localized, the lone pair is more available to accept a proton, which increases its basicity compared to aniline. Because benzylamine has a localized lone pair on the nitrogen, it is more basic than aniline. Thus, the answer is: Option D: Benzylamine.
questions.explanation_html:
Let's analyze each option by considering the availability of the nitrogen's lone pair for accepting a proton:

$\text{Aniline:}C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}$

In aniline, the lone pair on nitrogen is partially delocalized into the benzene ring. This delocalization makes the lone pair less available for protonation, so aniline is less basic compared to amines where the lone pair is fully localized.

$\text{Diphenylamine:}C_{6}H_{5}NHC_{6}H_{5}$

Here, the nitrogen is bonded to two phenyl groups. The lone pair can be delocalized into both aromatic rings, decreasing its availability even more than in aniline. This makes diphenylamine less basic.

$\text{Triphenylamine:}N(C_{6}H_{5})_{3}$

In triphenylamine, the nitrogen is bonded to three phenyl groups, which further delocalizes the lone pair into the aromatic rings. As a result, the lone pair is even less available, making triphenylamine even less basic.

$\text{Benzylamine:}C_{6}H_{5}CH_{2}NH_{2}$

In benzylamine, the nitrogen is attached to a methylene group ( $CH_{2}$ ) before connecting to the benzene ring. This extra methylene group breaks the conjugation between the benzene ring and the amine, keeping the lone pair localized on the nitrogen. Being more localized, the lone pair is more available to accept a proton, which increases its basicity compared to aniline.

Because benzylamine has a localized lone pair on the nitrogen, it is more basic than aniline.

Thus, the answer is:

Option D: Benzylamine.

questions.question_text: In which of the following, homolytic bond fission takes place?
questions.question_html: In which of the following, homolytic bond fission takes place?

options.label: A
options.html: Free radical chlorination of methane

options.label: B
options.text: Addition of HBr to double bond
options.html: Addition of HBr to double bond

options.label: C
options.html: Alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl chloride

options.label: D
options.html: Nitration of benzene

questions.explanation_text: In the process of free radical chlorination of methane, homolytic bond fission occurs during the initiation step. Here's a breakdown of the process: Initiation : The reaction begins with the homolytic cleavage of a chlorine molecule ( $Cl_{2}$ ) into two chlorine radicals ( $2Cl^{∙}$ ) under the influence of light: $Cl_{2}\overset{\text{Light}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}2Cl^{∙}$ Propagation : In the first propagation step, a chlorine radical reacts with a methane molecule ( $CH_{4}$ ), resulting in the formation of hydrogen chloride ( $HCl$ ) and a methyl radical ( $\overset{∙}{C}H_{3}$ ): $Cl+CH_{4} \longrightarrow HCl+\overset{∙}{C}H_{3}$ This methyl radical then reacts with another chlorine molecule, producing chloromethane ( $CH_{3}Cl$ ) and a new chlorine radical: $CH_{3}+Cl_{2} \longrightarrow CH_{3}Cl+Cl^{∙}$ Termination : Termination occurs when two radicals combine to form a stable molecule, halting the chain reaction. Possible termination steps include: $\begin{aligned} 2Cl^{∙} & \longrightarrow Cl_{2} \\ Cl^{∙}+\overset{∙}{C}H_{3} & \longrightarrow CH_{3}Cl \\ 2\overset{∙}{C}H_{3} & \longrightarrow CH_{3}CH_{3} \end{aligned}$ In this mechanism, homolytic fission is a critical step that begins the chain reaction, allowing the formation of radicals necessary for further reaction steps.
questions.explanation_html:
In the process of free radical chlorination of methane, homolytic bond fission occurs during the initiation step. Here's a breakdown of the process:

Initiation:

The reaction begins with the homolytic cleavage of a chlorine molecule ( $Cl_{2}$ ) into two chlorine radicals ( $2Cl^{∙}$ ) under the influence of light:

$Cl_{2}\overset{\text{Light}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}2Cl^{∙}$

Propagation:

In the first propagation step, a chlorine radical reacts with a methane molecule ( $CH_{4}$ ), resulting in the formation of hydrogen chloride ( $HCl$ ) and a methyl radical ( $\overset{∙}{C}H_{3}$ ):

$Cl+CH_{4} \longrightarrow HCl+\overset{∙}{C}H_{3}$

This methyl radical then reacts with another chlorine molecule, producing chloromethane ( $CH_{3}Cl$ ) and a new chlorine radical:

$CH_{3}+Cl_{2} \longrightarrow CH_{3}Cl+Cl^{∙}$

Termination:

Termination occurs when two radicals combine to form a stable molecule, halting the chain reaction. Possible termination steps include:

$\begin{aligned} 2Cl^{∙} & \longrightarrow Cl_{2} \\ Cl^{∙}+\overset{∙}{C}H_{3} & \longrightarrow CH_{3}Cl \\ 2\overset{∙}{C}H_{3} & \longrightarrow CH_{3}CH_{3} \end{aligned}$

In this mechanism, homolytic fission is a critical step that begins the chain reaction, allowing the formation of radicals necessary for further reaction steps.
